newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela accuses West of demonising Congo's Kabila.
newsitem.headline: Mandela accuses West of demonising Congo's Kabila.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela on Tuesday accused Western governments of demonising self-proclaimed president Laurent Kabila of the Democratic Republic of Congo and said the former rebel leader had his full trust.
Mandela, who played a key role in negotiations between Kabila and ousted Zairean president Mobutu Sese Seko, said the renamed country's new leader had demonstrated a commitment to democracy.

"It does appear to me that he (Kabila) has been so demonised by Western governments that even his achievements have not been noticed," Mandela told reporters after talks with visiting Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni.
"What he has done in the areas that he has conquered shows very clearly his commitment to democracy."
Kabila has been widely recognised as leader of the Democratic Republic of Congo, but Western media and governments have urged him to demonstrate a commitment to democracy and human rights.
Some aid agencies working in the country, the third-biggest in Africa, have accused his followers of atrocities against refugees mainly in the southeast.
Mandela and Museveni defended Kabila's suspension on Monday of political activity in Kinshasa, but the South African leader said he was confident the ban was temporary.
"You must judge what president Kabila is doing against the specific conditions existing in that country.
"There is a great deal of disorganisation in that country. It would be suicidal for him to allow the operation of parties before he has a firm grip on the government of the country.
"I think therefore that we can trust him, on the basis of his record, to keep his word," Mandela said.

Museveni said he had taken similar action against political parties in his own country and believed that largely rural African societies, which he called pre-industrial, were not ready for multi-party democracy.
"I myself don't like political parties...I restricted their activities. If Mr Kabila copies that type of situation, I wouldn't be surprised," he said.
Mandela said he had spoken to leaders throughout central Africa and in Europe to ensure a united approach to peacemaking in the former Zaire.

"I briefed them and was able to get support for the initiative South Africa had taken in the Congo. Therefore, I have no doubt that the support of the leaders that surround the Democratic Republic of the Congo will eventually bring about stability in that country."
Mandela said he was willing to accept Kabila's judgment in excluding former popular prime minister Etienne Tshisekedi from his transitional adminsitration.
"I would leave the matter to the man on the spot. He (Kabila) knows the leaders in that country. I am prepared to be guided by president Kabila in regard to the situation in that country," he said.
